titre: A 1964 Sound Illusion Structures the Script of Dunkirk
accroche: A note seems to rise forever, never reaching a peak, and yet it never leaves its own register.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1964, the American researcher Roger Shepard, then at Bell Labs, publishes in the Journal of the Acoustical Society of America a paper on a phenomenon he has just produced by computer: a series of sounds that seems to rise endlessly in pitch, without ever exceeding a given register. The trick lies in superposition. Each sound in the series is not a single frequency but a stack of several frequencies separated pairwise by an exact octave. As the series rises, the highest frequencies fade out gradually while new low frequencies appear beneath, invisible to the ear because they come in playing very softly. One hears a continuous ascent; what one cannot hear is where it starts over.

## A sound ribbon folded back on itself

The French composer Jean-Claude Risset extends the idea by making the glide continuous rather than in steps, what is now called the Shepard-Risset glissando. In both versions, the principle recalls a Penrose staircase in painting: each step, taken in isolation, is coherent, but the whole closes back on itself without one being able to spot where. The ear, used to judging the pitch of a sound by its frequency, lets itself be guided by the movement of the sound envelope rather than by the frequency itself, and perceives a motion that, strictly speaking, goes nowhere.

## What it shifts

In 2017, director Christopher Nolan pushes the principle beyond the score. He explains in an interview that the script of *Dunkirk* interweaves three timelines (a week on the beach, a day at sea, an hour in the air) according to this same principle of continuous ascent, for a tension that rises without ever falling back or resolving: the narrative structure reproduces, scene after scene, what the Shepard tone does to the ear. Nolan had already explored the idea in 2006 with composer David Julyan on *The Prestige*, before entrusting it to Hans Zimmer, who builds the entire score of *Dunkirk* around a ticking watch that, likewise, never stops. An illusion born in a hearing-research laboratory thus becomes a principle of staging: sustaining a tension that never resolves, without the viewer being able to say why it does not fall back.

quiz.question: Why does the Shepard tone give the illusion of a pitch that rises forever?
choix: Because the frequency of the sound really does increase continuously, without ever stopping
Because frequencies separated by octaves rise together, the high ones fading out beneath new low ones
Because the recording is sped up with each repetition, as on a vinyl turntable
Because the human ear systematically confuses two notes less than an octave apart
quiz.explication: The Shepard tone superposes frequencies each spaced an exact octave apart: as the series rises, the high frequencies fade out softly while new low frequencies appear beneath, with no audible break. The frequency therefore does not climb forever, contrary to what one hears: nothing is sped up as on a record, and the ear distinguishes octaves very well. It is only guided by the sound envelope rather than by the absolute frequency.
